A surplice is a loose, white garment worn by certain people during Christian religious services. Think of it as a special piece of clothing that signals, "I have a role in this ceremony."

Picture a wide, flowing white top — almost like an oversized white shirt or a short white robe. It falls roughly to the hips or knees, depending on the tradition. Its most distinctive feature is its wide, flowing sleeves, which are noticeably roomier than a normal shirt's sleeves. The fabric is typically white linen or cotton, and in some traditions, the hem and sleeves are decorated with lace or embroidery. Overall, it gives an impression of flowing, ceremonial whiteness.

A surplice is worn during church services, mainly in Western Christian traditions such as Roman Catholic, Anglican/Episcopal, and Lutheran churches. The people most commonly seen wearing one include:

  • Clergy — priests, deacons, and ministers
  • Choir members — the singers who perform during the service
  • Altar servers (acolytes) — people who assist the priest at the altar
  • Lay readers — non-clergy members who read scripture aloud during the service

It is not everyday clothing. It is put on specifically for the duration of a religious ceremony and taken off afterward.

A surplice is almost never worn alone as the only garment. It is layered on top of other vestments (the general word for special religious clothing). Most commonly, it goes over a cassock — a long, plain robe that extends all the way to the floor, usually black or dark-coloured. The white surplice over the dark cassock is one of the most recognizable sights in a traditional church choir or clergy procession.

The white colour is symbolic. In Christian tradition, white stands for purity, holiness, and consecration (being set apart for a sacred purpose). By wearing a surplice, the person is visually marking themselves as someone who is set apart from the congregation for a specific role in the service. It is a uniform, in a sense — one that communicates both function and reverence.
How it differs from similar garments

Since a surplice is one of several white religious garments, it helps to know what it is not:

  • An alb is also a white garment, but it is a full-length robe reaching all the way to the feet, more form-fitting, and typically worn by the priest specifically for the Eucharist (Communion). A surplice is shorter and much looser.
  • A chasuble is a large, poncho-like outer vestment worn over everything else by a priest celebrating Mass. It is usually colourful (not white by default) and shaped very differently.
  • A cope is a long, cape-like ceremonial cloak. Very different in shape.

The surplice is specifically the shorter, wide-sleeved, loose white layer worn by choir members, acolytes, and lesser clergy — not typically the main celebrant's most formal vestment.

The choirboys straightened their surplices before filing into the cathedral.

The deacon wore a black cassock beneath his white surplice.

She had worn a surplice as an altar server throughout her childhood.

A surplice is a loose, wide-sleeved, white liturgical garment worn over a cassock by clergy, choir members, and altar servers during Christian worship services, symbolizing purity and a designated role in the ceremony.
